idiom_name: a stateless contract type (operations only) plus implementations handed out as that type
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare a named type that contains only operation signatures — no fields, no constructor, no body that ties the role to a representation — and let every supplier implement it; clients hold values of the contract type and receive them from a factory so the concrete type stays private. Combine contracts by type-set composition (base-interface extension, several interfaces per class, trait or protocol composition) rather than through a shared state-carrying base. Write the semantics — pre/postconditions, allowed errors, thread-safety, lifetime, nullability — next to the contract because no compiler checks them. Where the language has static contracts (generic bounds, concepts, type sets), use them for implementors known at compile time; reserve runtime dispatch (trait objects, vtable, boxed values) for implementors that arrive at run time or from separate teams. Go's practice of placing the interface in the consuming package and returning concrete types lets implementors add methods without breaking clients — apply this principle wherever the language allows it. Rust's sealed-trait pattern (C-SEALED) allows a published contract to gain members non-destructively: a private empty supertrait prevents downstream from implementing the contract, granting the author freedom to add members without a breaking change. Swift's protocol extensions with default implementations allow the same additive freedom; Kotlin, C# (DIM) and Java (default methods) provide the same capability with different dispatch semantics. Design the contract from the caller's side: a role interface answers only the operations a specific client needs in one interaction, not the full public surface of any existing class. Wire implementations at a single composition root; libraries should expose contracts (and optionally Abstract Factories or Facades) but must never own a composition root — that belongs to the application entry point.
code_sketch:
contract Shape                  # operations only: no state, no constructor
    area() -> double            # every implementation must provide these
    draw()

implementation Square : Shape    # state lives in the implementation
    side: double
    area() -> side * side
    draw()

provider make_square(side) -> Shape   # clients never name Square
pitfalls: Letting the contract grow a field or a constructor turns it back into a base class and re-couples every client to a representation.
Publishing the implementation type next to the contract invites construction and downcasts at the call site - the substitutability the contract existed for is lost.
A contract that merely restates one implementation's public methods adds indirection without substitutability; design it from the caller's role instead.
Publishing the implementation type next to the contract invites construction and downcasts at the call site — the substitutability the contract existed for is lost.

Additive change without a default body breaks every implementation — the language's non-breaking growth mechanism (default/extension members, DIM, sealed traits) must be used or a new versioned contract published.
Default-method collision (two interfaces with conflicting defaults) signals a contract design problem; the compiler forces an override which reveals the conflict.

A class does not inherit interface members in C# — variables must be typed as the interface to call contract methods, so tests constructing the real class cannot invoke contract behaviour without a cast.
Hyrum's Law: with enough users, every observable behaviour of every implementation becomes a de-facto contract; silent implementation changes break consumers who depended on undocumented behaviour.
An interface with a single capability probe operation is better expressed as a capability query; a contract over synchronous one-off calls is better as a function value.

Marker interfaces (Cloneable, Serializable) force every implementor to satisfy the marker's contract; language metadata attributes express the same intent without the type-level commitment and are easier to remove later.
Composition Root belongs only to applications — libraries and frameworks that define their own composition root force consumers to adopt a specific DI container or architecture.

Wrong move: extract an interface mechanically from every public member of one class -> the contract leaks representation and forces clients to depend on irrelevant operations -> instead define a role-sized contract from the consuming interaction.

Wrong move: let clients discover and construct concrete providers ad hoc -> replacement, decoration, and testing require edits at every call site -> instead select and hand out providers at one composition boundary as the contract type.

Wrong move: add a required operation to a published interface without a compatibility plan -> existing implementors fail to compile or receive unsafe defaults -> instead use a default/extension member where semantics permit or publish a new versioned contract.
